title: Angle Bisector — Verifying with the tan θ Method
topicTitle: Pair of straight lines: general equation of second degree in x and y, condition for representing a pair of lines, homogenous second-degree equation in x and y, angle between pair of lines, bisectors of the angles between pair of lines
notes: As a cross-check, find the angle θ between one of the original lines and one candidate bisector using: tan θ = |(m₁ − m_b)/(1 + m₁·m_b)|, where m₁ is the original line's slope and m_b is the bisector's slope
**If tan θ < 1** (θ < 45°): since θ is half the angle between the two original lines, the total angle is less than 90°, so this bisector is the **acute** angle bisector
**If tan θ > 1** (θ > 45°): this bisector is the **obtuse** angle bisector
**Worked check:** slope of Bisector 1 (6x + 6y − 1 = 0) is m_b = −6/6 = −1; with the original line's slope m₁ = −1/2: tan θ = |(−1/2 − (−1))/(1 + (−1/2)(−1))| = |(1/2)/(3/2)| = 1/3
Since tan θ = 1/3 < 1, this confirms 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 is definitively the **acute angle bisector** — matching the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method
**Angle between two lines formula:** For lines with slopes m₁ and m₂: $$\tan \theta = \left| \frac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1 m_2} \right|$$
**When the bisector is at exactly 45° to the original line**, the two original lines are perpendicular (angle between them is 90°). This happens when a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 0.
**Special case:** If one of the original lines is vertical (undefined slope), use the angle formula θ = |90° − tan⁻¹(m)| or work directly with the angle from the x-axis.
**Summary of two methods:** (1) a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method: fast, direct, no slope computation needed. (2) tan θ verification: universal, works as a cross-check, but requires slope computation.

**Key insight:** The bisector divides the angle between two lines into two equal parts. If the angle between the lines is θ, each half-angle is θ/2. So tan(θ/2) < 1 means θ < 90° (acute), and tan(θ/2) > 1 means θ > 90° (obtuse).
confusion: tan θ < 1 does NOT mean the angle is small in absolute terms — it means θ < 45°, which means the full angle between the lines is < 90° (acute).
When using the tan θ formula, always take the absolute value. The unsigned angle between lines is always between 0° and 90° by convention.
Do not confuse the angle between a bisector and one original line (θ/2) with the angle between the two original lines (θ). The bisector formula gives you the half-angle.
If m₁ · m₂ = −1, the lines are perpendicular and tan θ is undefined (infinite) — this means θ = 90°.
practice: Verify that the obtuse bisector 2x − 2y + 19 = 0 makes an angle > 45° with the line −x − 2y + 3 = 0.
Find the acute angle bisector of y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 3 using both the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method and tan θ verification.
Show that if the angle between two lines is 60°, then each bisector makes an angle of 30° with the original lines.
universalFacts: The tan θ method is universally applicable to any pair of lines, while the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ shortcut requires lines in standard form with positive constants.
When the angle between lines is exactly 90°, both bisectors are at 45° and neither is acute nor obtuse.
In competitive exams, the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method is preferred for speed, while the tan θ method is preferred for verification.
